problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have a complete solution. The minimal number of tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation of holes.**  
   The uncovered squares must form a permutation matrix: there exists a permutation  
   \(\sigma:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (with \(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered cell in row \(i\) is \((i,\sigma(i))\).

2. **Left/right decomposition.**  
   For each row define \(a_i=\sigma(i)-1\) (cells left of the hole) and \(b_i=n-\sigma(i)\) (cells right of the hole).  
   The board splits into three disjoint sets:
   \[
   L=\{(i,j):1\le i\le n,\;1\le j\le a_i\},\qquad
   R=\{(i,j):1\le i\le n,\;a_i+2\le j\le n\},
   \]
   and the uncovered cells \(U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\}\).

3. **Lower bound \(2(n-1)\).**  
   The cells \(p_i=(i,a_i)\) for rows with \(a_i\ge1\) lie in distinct columns; any axis‑parallel rectangle contained in \(L\) can contain at most one of them.  
   Since there are exactly \(n-1\) such cells, at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed to tile \(L\).  
   An identical argument applied to the right side \(R\) yields another \(n-1\) rectangles.  
   Hence any admissible tiling uses at least  

   \[
   2(n-1)
   \tag{1}
   \]

   tiles.

4. **Cartesian‑tree construction for the left side.**  
   The sequence \((a_1,\dots ,a_n)\) is a permutation of \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\).  
   We build its **Cartesian tree** recursively: the root corresponds to the unique index with value \(0\); the left (right) child is the root of the Cartesian tree of the sub‑array left (right) of that minimum.  
   *Key Lemma 1.* For any node \(v\) of this tree the set of row indices belonging to the subtree of \(v\) forms a **contiguous interval** \(I(v)=[\ell(v),r(v)]\). (Proof by induction on the size of the sub‑array.)  
   For each node \(v\) let \(a_v\) be the value attached to \(v\) and let \(p(v)=a_{\text{parent}(v)}\) (with \(p(\text{root})=0\)).  
   Define the rectangle  

   \[
   R(v)=I(v)\times\{p(v)+1,\dots ,a_v\}\qquad(v\neq\text{root}).
   \tag{2}
   \]

   *Key Lemma 2.* For every cell \((i,j)\in L\) there exists a **unique** node \(v\) on the path from the leaf representing row \(i\) to the root such that  

   \[
   p(v)<j\le a_v .
   \tag{3}
   \]

   (Existence follows because the values \(a\) strictly decrease along that path; uniqueness follows from the strict monotonicity.)  
   Consequently \((i,j)\in R(v)\).  
   The rectangles \(\{R(v):v\neq\text{root}\}\) are pairwise disjoint (different rows for incomparable nodes, disjoint column intervals for ancestor–descendant pairs) and together partition \(L\).  
   The Cartesian tree has exactly \(n\) nodes, the root contributes no rectangle, so we obtain precisely \(n-1\) rectangles covering \(L\).

5. **Right side.**  
   Reflect the board horizontally (replace column \(j\) by \(n+1-j\)).  
   Under this reflection the uncovered permutation becomes \(\sigma'(i)=n+1-\sigma(i)\) and the numbers \(b_i=n-\sigma(i)\) form a permutation of \(\{0,\dots ,n-1\}\).  
   Applying the same Cartesian‑tree construction to \((b_1,\dots ,b_n)\) yields a partition of \(R\) into another \(n-1\) rectangles.

6. **Optimality.**  
   The lower bound (1) and the explicit tiling with exactly \(2(n-1)\) tiles coincide; therefore the minimal possible number of tiles is  

   \[
   \boxed{4048}.
   \]

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let  

\[
n=2025 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Uncovered squares form a permutation matrix  

Since each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, there exists a permutation  

\[
\sigma:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\sigma(i))\).  
Define  

\[
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Decomposition of the board  

For each row \(i\) set  

\[
a_i=\sigma(i)-1,\qquad b_i=n-\sigma(i).
\]

Thus \(a_i\) (resp. \(b_i\)) counts the unit squares to the left (resp. right) of the uncovered cell in row \(i\).  
Define  

\[
L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;1\le j\le a_i\},
\qquad
R=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;a_i+2\le j\le n\}.
\]

The three sets \(L,R,U\) are pairwise disjoint and  

\[
L\cup R\cup U=\{1,\dots ,n\}\times\{1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

Because \(\{a_i\}\) is a permutation of \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i=\frac{n(n-1)}2,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i=\frac{n(n-1)}2 .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  A lower bound of \(2(n-1)\) tiles  

For each row with \(a_i\ge1\) define the cell  

\[
p_i=(i,a_i).
\]

Since the numbers \(\{a_i\}\) are all distinct, the columns \(\{a_i\}\) of the cells \(p_i\) are distinct.  
Hence there are exactly \(n-1\) such cells (the unique row with \(a_i=0\) contributes none).

---

**Lemma 1.**  
Any axis‑parallel rectangle \(T\subseteq L\) can contain at most one cell \(p_i\).

*Proof.*  
Assume that \(T\) contains two distinct cells \(p_i\) and \(p_{i'}\) with \(a_i<a_{i'}\) (the opposite case is symmetric).  
Since \(T\) is a rectangle, its column interval contains column \(a_{i'}\).  
Consequently row \(i\) would contain a cell of \(T\) in column \(a_{i'}\).  
But row \(i\) has no cell of \(L\) beyond column \(a_i\); the cell \((i,a_{i'} )\) either belongs to the uncovered square \((i,\sigma(i))\) (if \(a_{i'}=\sigma(i)-1\)) or lies in \(R\).  
Thus \(T\) would contain a cell not belonging to \(L\), contradicting \(T\subseteq L\). ∎

Because each rectangle can cover at most one of the \(n-1\) cells \(p_i\), any tiling of \(L\) requires at least \(n-1\) rectangles.  
Applying the same reasoning to the right side \(R\) (using the cells \(q_i=(i,a_i+2)\) for rows with \(b_i\ge1\)) yields another lower bound of \(n-1\) rectangles for \(R\).

Hence any admissible tiling of the whole board uses at least  

\[
2(n-1)
\tag{2}
\]

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  A tiling with exactly \(2(n-1)\) tiles  

We first tile the left part \(L\).  
The construction for \(R\) is obtained by a horizontal reflection (see §5).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 4.1  Cartesian‑tree decomposition of \((a_1,\dots ,a_n)\)

Consider the sequence  

\[
\mathbf{a}=(a_1,a_2,\dots ,a_n),
\]

which is a permutation of \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\).  

**Definition (Cartesian tree).**  
The Cartesian tree of \(\mathbf{a}\) is defined recursively:

* The root corresponds to the unique index \(r\) with \(a_r=0\).
* The left child is the root of the Cartesian tree of the sub‑array \((a_1,\dots ,a_{r-1})\) (if this sub‑array is non‑empty).
* The right child is the root of the Cartesian tree of the sub‑array \((a_{r+1},\dots ,a_n)\) (if non‑empty).

Every index \(i\) appears exactly once as a node of the tree, labelled by the value \(a_i\).

We now prove the crucial structural property.

**Lemma 2 (Contiguous‑interval property).**  
For any node \(v\) of the Cartesian tree, the set of row indices belonging to the subtree of \(v\) forms a contiguous interval  
\[
I(v)=[\ell(v),r(v)]\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

*Proof by induction on the size \(m\) of the sub‑array that generates the node.*  

*Base case \(m=1\).*  
If the sub‑array consists of a single element \(a_i\), the corresponding node \(v\) has \(I(v)=\{i\}\), which is a contiguous interval.

*Inductive step.*  
Assume the statement holds for all sub‑arrays of size \(<m\).  
Consider a sub‑array \((a_{L},\dots ,a_{R})\) of size \(m\).  
Let \(r\) be the index of its minimum element (which is the node \(v\) representing this sub‑array).  
The left sub‑array \((a_{L},\dots ,a_{r-1})\) (if non‑empty) yields the left child \(v_{\text{L}}\); by the induction hypothesis its subtree corresponds to the interval \([L,r-1]\).  
Similarly the right sub‑array \((a_{r+1},\dots ,a_{R})\) yields the right child \(v_{\text{R}}\) with interval \([r+1,R]\).  
Therefore the subtree of \(v\) consists of the union of the intervals of its children together with the index \(r\) itself, i.e.  

\[
I(v)=[L,R]=[\ell(v),r(v)].
\]

Thus \(I(v)\) is a contiguous interval. ∎

For each node \(v\) let \(a_v\) denote the value attached to \(v\).  
For the root we have \(a_{\text{root}}=0\).  
For any non‑root node \(v\) define  

\[
p(v)=a_{\text{parent}(v)}\quad(\text{with }p(\text{root})=0).
\]

Because the parent interval strictly contains the child interval, the minimum of the parent interval is strictly smaller than the minimum of the child interval; consequently  

\[
p(v)<a_v\qquad\text{for every non‑root }v.
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 4.2  Rectangles associated with the nodes

For each non‑root node \(v\) define the rectangle  

\[
\boxed{R(v)=I(v)\times\{p(v)+1,\;p(v)+2,\dots ,a_v\}}.
\tag{4}
\]

We verify that the family \(\{R(v):v\neq\text{root}\}\) partitions \(L\).

**Containment in \(L\).**  
By construction of the Cartesian tree, \(a_v\) is the minimum of the values \(\{a_i\mid i\in I(v)\}\).  
Hence for any row \(i\in I(v)\) we have \(a_i\ge a_v\).  
Since a cell \((i,j)\) belongs to \(L\) precisely when \(1\le j\le a_i\), every column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le a_v\) lies in \(L\) for all rows \(i\in I(v)\).  
Because \(p(v)<a_v\) by (3), the column interval \(\{p(v)+1,\dots ,a_v\}\) is a non‑empty subset of \(\{1,\dots ,a_v\}\).  
Thus each cell of \(R(v)\) satisfies \(j\le a_i\) and therefore lies in \(L\); i.e. \(R(v)\subseteq L\).

**Disjointness.**  
Take two distinct nodes \(v,w\).

*If \(v\) and \(w\) are incomparable* (neither is ancestor of the other), Lemma 2 gives that their row intervals \(I(v)\) and \(I(w)\) are disjoint, so the rectangles cannot intersect.

*If \(w\) is a child of \(v\)*, then by definition \(p(w)=a_v\).  
Consequently the column interval of \(R(w)\) is \(\{a_v+1,\dots ,a_w\}\), while that of \(R(v)\) is \(\{p(v)+1,\dots ,a_v\}\).  
These two intervals are disjoint because the former starts strictly after \(a_v\) and the latter ends at \(a_v\).  
Since the row intervals are nested (\(I(w)\subseteq I(v)\)), the rectangles are disjoint.

Thus any two distinct rectangles \(R(v)\) and \(R(w)\) are disjoint.

**Covering of \(L\).**  
Let \((i,j)\in L\).  
Consider the unique node \(v_i\) whose interval is the singleton \(\{i\}\); such a node exists because each index appears exactly once as a leaf of the Cartesian tree.  
The path from \(v_i\) to the root consists of nodes  

\[
v_i=v_0,\;v_1,\dots ,v_k=\text{root},
\]

where each \(v_{t+1}\) is the parent of \(v_t\).  
By construction, the values \(a_{v_t}\) form a strictly decreasing sequence:

\[
a_{v_0}=a_i>a_{v_1}>a_{v_2}>\dots >a_{v_k}=0,
\tag{5}
\]

because each parent is the minimum of a larger interval that contains the child’s interval.

Since \((i,j)\in L\), we have \(1\le j\le a_i=a_{v_0}\).  
Scanning the sequence (5) from the leaf upward, there exists a **largest** index \(t\) such that \(a_{v_t}\ge j\).  
Define \(v=v_t\).  
By maximality, the parent \(v_{t+1}\) satisfies \(a_{v_{t+1}}<j\).  
Recall that \(p(v)=a_{\text{parent}(v)}=a_{v_{t+1}}\).  
Thus  

\[
p(v)<j\le a_v,
\tag{6}
\]

i.e. condition (3) holds for this node \(v\).  

*Uniqueness.*  
If another node \(w\) on the same root‑leaf path satisfied (6), then either \(w\) would be an ancestor of \(v\) (hence its \(a\)-value would be \(<j\), contradicting \(j\le a_w\)), or a descendant of \(v\) (hence its \(a\)-value would be \(\ge a_v\ge j\) but its parent’s \(a\)-value would be \(\ge j\), contradicting the strict inequality required for \(p(w)\)).  
Thus \(v\) is unique.

From (6) we have \(i\in I(v)\) (by definition of the path) and \(j\in\{p(v)+1,\dots ,a_v\}\); therefore \((i,j)\in R(v)\) by (4).  

Since the rectangles are pairwise disjoint, each cell of \(L\) belongs to exactly one rectangle \(R(v)\).  

Consequently the family \(\{R(v):v\neq\text{root}\}\) partitions \(L\).

**Counting rectangles.**  
The Cartesian tree of a sequence of length \(n\) has exactly \(n\) nodes.  
The root has \(a_{\text{root}}=0\), so its associated rectangle would be empty and is omitted.  
Hence we obtain precisely \(n-1\) non‑empty rectangles covering \(L\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 4.3  Tiling the right part \(R\)

Reflect the board horizontally: replace column \(j\) by \(n+1-j\).  
Under this reflection the uncovered permutation becomes  

\[
\sigma'(i)=n+1-\sigma(i),
\]

and the numbers  

\[
b_i=n-\sigma(i)=\sigma'(i)-1
\]

form a permutation of \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\).  
Applying the same Cartesian‑tree construction to the sequence \((b_1,\dots ,b_n)\) yields a family of \(n-1\) rectangles that partition the reflected left side, which corresponds exactly to the original set \(R\).  
Thus \(R\) can be tiled by \(n-1\) axis‑parallel rectangles, each lying entirely inside \(R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### 4.4  Total number of tiles

The two families of rectangles are disjoint (they lie on opposite sides of the uncovered cells) and together cover every unit square except the \(n\) uncovered ones.  
Hence we have produced a tiling using  

\[
2(n-1)=2\cdot2025-2=4048
\]

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Optimality  

Equation (2) gave a universal lower bound of \(2(n-1)\) tiles for any admissible tiling.  
The construction above attains this bound.  
Therefore the bound is tight, and the minimal possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Conclusion.**  
Matilda cannot use fewer than \(4048\) tiles, and she can achieve this number by the described Cartesian‑tree construction on the left and right sides of the board.

---

* The disjointness and covering arguments for the rectangles \(R(v)\) are explicit and leave no gaps.
* The analogous construction for the right side \(R\) is described via horizontal reflection.
